title: Variables and types of data
summary: Quantitative vs qualitative variables, grouped classifications, the types-of-data tree, and the mapping exercise with its solution.

chunks.heading: Quantitative and qualitative variables
chunks.explanation_md:
The slide sorts everyday **variables** into two groups:

- **Quantitative:** height, weight, age, temperature, income.
- **Qualitative:** educational qualification, gender, and your LMTSM experience on a scale of 1-5 (1 = Very bad to 5 = Excellent).

The LMTSM experience item is circled: even though it uses numbers 1 to 5, the numbers are **labels for categories** (very bad, bad, good...), so it is **qualitative**.
chunks.exam_line: Height, weight, age, temperature and income are quantitative; educational qualification, gender and a 1-5 experience rating are qualitative.

chunks.heading: Grouping numbers into classes
chunks.explanation_md:
Numbers are often **grouped into classes**, which turns them into ordered categories:

- **Weight:** 40-45, 45-50, ... 95-100.
- **Farmers by land:** marginal (up to 1 hectares), small (1 to 2), medium (2 to 4), big (above 4 hectares).
- **Revised MSME classification** (investment and annual turnover): Micro: investment < Rs. 1 cr and turnover < Rs. 5 cr; Small: investment < Rs. 10 cr and turnover < Rs. 50 cr; Medium: investment < Rs. 20 cr and turnover < Rs. 100 cr.
- **Education levels:** E0 illiterate (no schooling) up to E5 (more than 11 years of schooling).
chunks.exam_line: Grouped classes (weight bands, farmer sizes, MSME categories, education levels E0 to E5) turn numbers into ordered categories.

chunks.heading: The types of data tree
chunks.explanation_md:
**Data** splits into two branches, each with two types:

- **Categorical (qualitative):** **Nominal** (names, no order) and **Ordinal** (ordered categories).
- **Numerical (quantitative):** **Discrete** (counts) and **Continuous** (measurements).

The slide's mapping exercise (25 items) and its solution:

| Nominal | Ordinal | Discrete | Continuous |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hair colour, gender, roll number, nationality, relationship status, blood type, preferred mode of transport, food preferred, movie genres, class section, pin code | Educational level, socio-economic status, consumer satisfaction | Number of stars in a movie, size of the class, number of children, total number of trees, runs scored, balls faced, total wickets taken | Height of a person, length of your arm, weight of a person, strike rate |

Watch the traps: **roll number and pin code are nominal** (numbers used as labels), and **strike rate is continuous**.
chunks.exam_line: Categorical data is nominal or ordinal; numerical data is discrete or continuous (roll number and pin code are nominal; runs scored is discrete; strike rate is continuous).

questions.stem: 'Your LMTSM experience on a scale of 1-5' uses numbers. Explain why the slide still classifies it as qualitative.
questions.model_answer_md:
Numbers do not automatically make a variable quantitative.

- The item is scored **1 = Very bad, 2 = Bad, 3 = Good, 4 = Very Good, 5 = Excellent**.
- The numbers are **labels for categories**, not measured amounts, so the slide circles it with the **qualitative** group (with educational qualification and gender).
- The categories have an order, so it is the same kind of item as **consumer satisfaction**, which the mapping solution puts under **ordinal**.

So it is qualitative (categorical) data with an order.

rubric.point: Scale 1 to 5 maps to very bad to excellent
Numbers are labels for categories, so qualitative
Ordered categories, like consumer satisfaction (ordinal)

questions.stem: Draw the types-of-data tree and classify these items from the slide's exercise, giving a reason for each: hair colour, roll number, educational level, consumer satisfaction, number of children, runs scored, height of a person, strike rate.
questions.model_answer_md:
Every data item first goes into one of two branches, then one of two types.

**The tree:**
- **Data**
  - **Categorical (qualitative)**: **Nominal** (labels, no order) and **Ordinal** (ordered categories)
  - **Numerical (quantitative)**: **Discrete** (counts) and **Continuous** (measurements)

**Classification:**

| Item | Type | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Hair colour | **Nominal** | A name with no order |
| Roll number | **Nominal** | A number used only as a label |
| Educational level | **Ordinal** | Levels have a clear order |
| Consumer satisfaction | **Ordinal** | Ordered ratings of satisfaction |
| Number of children | **Discrete** | Counted in whole numbers |
| Runs scored | **Discrete** | Counted |
| Height of a person | **Continuous** | Measured |
| Strike rate | **Continuous** | Calculated, not counted, and can take any value |

**The two traps the solution teaches:**
- **Numbers can be nominal:** roll number and pin code look numerical, but you cannot add or rank them meaningfully; they only identify.
- **Cricket items split:** runs scored, balls faced and wickets are discrete counts, but **strike rate** is continuous.

**Conclusion:** ask first whether the value is a label or an amount, then whether the label has an order or the amount is counted or measured.

rubric.point: Tree: categorical (nominal, ordinal) and numerical (discrete, continuous)
Hair colour and roll number nominal
Educational level and consumer satisfaction ordinal
Number of children and runs scored discrete
Height and strike rate continuous
Reasons: label vs amount; counted vs measured

questions.stem: Differentiate between quantitative and qualitative variables. Use the slide's list of everyday variables and explain the traps where numbers appear in qualitative data or where counts and measurements differ.
questions.model_answer_md:
Variables are first split by whether they record an **amount** or a **category**.

| Basis | Quantitative (numerical) | Qualitative (categorical) |
|---|---|---|
| **Records** | Amounts that are counted or measured | Categories or labels |
| **Types** | **Discrete** and **continuous** | **Nominal** and **ordinal** |
| **Slide's variables** | Height, weight, age (# of years), temperature, income | Educational qualification, gender, LMTSM experience on a 1-5 scale |

**Trap 1: numbers used as labels.** The **LMTSM experience scale** (1 = Very bad up to 5 = Excellent) is **qualitative**, because the numbers name categories. **Roll number** and **pin code** are **nominal** for the same reason.

**Trap 2: counted vs measured.** Within quantitative data, counts such as **number of children, runs scored, balls faced** are **discrete**; measurements such as **height, weight, length of arm** and **strike rate** are **continuous**.

**Trap 3: grouping.** A quantitative variable can be **grouped into classes**: weight into 40-45, 45-50 and so on, or farmers into marginal, small, medium and big by hectares. The classes are ordered categories.

**Conclusion:** classify by what the value means, not by whether it is written as a number.

rubric.point: Quantitative: amounts; discrete and continuous
Qualitative: categories; nominal and ordinal
Slide's lists of quantitative and qualitative variables
LMTSM 1-5 scale is qualitative; roll number and pin code nominal
Counts discrete vs measurements continuous (strike rate)
Grouping into classes, e.g. weight or farmer classes
